text.problem.bad2: Absolute paths point at the drive root

text.problem.good3: Same tab, same profile, your browser
text.how.title: Three steps, none of them yours
text.how.lead: Fenestra attaches itself to the double-click and decides what the file needs.
text.how.s1d: Double-click it, drag the folder onto the executable, or pass a path on the command line.
text.how.s2d: It reads the HTML. Needs an HTTP origin? It starts a server on a stable port. Does not? It opens the file directly.
text.how.s3d: A normal tab, in your window, with your profile, your extensions and your address bar.
text.compat.title: What works, what does not
text.compat.lead:
If the folder works on any static host, it works here. If it needs a build step or a
          backend, it does not — and Fenestra says so instead of failing silently.
text.compat.c1: Plain HTML, CSS and JS served from the folder.
text.compat.c2: Extensionless paths fall back to index.html, so refresh works.
text.compat.c3: Opened directly by Edge through file://, with no server at all.
text.compat.c4: Source projects need their own dev server to compile.
text.compat.c5: Fenestra serves files. It does not proxy, run services or touch a database.
text.compat.c6: The root is the file's folder, and .. is confined for safety.
text.plat.title: One idea, three systems
text.plat.lead:
Same job everywhere: turn a folder into localhost and open it in your browser.
          The packaging changes because each system has its own rules.
text.plat.win.desc: A single ~120 KB executable. No installer, no runtime — .NET Framework 4.8 already ships with Windows.
text.plat.linux.desc: One static binary, no runtime, for amd64 and arm64.
text.plat.macos.desc: No notarized app bundle: the CLI installs via Homebrew, the Finder app you build locally.
text.plat.note: Every release also ships the complete source as zip and tar.gz. Nothing here is closed.
text.install.title: One file. No installer.
text.install.lead: Pick the package for your system. Every one of them is a single file — no installer, no runtime.
text.install.dlText: The ~120 KB .exe above runs as-is. No installer, no runtime.
text.install.signNote:
The binary is not code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen will ask for confirmation
              once. That is expected for an alpha build.
text.install.defText: One time, three clicks. Windows does not let an app do this alone.
text.install.note:
Windows allows exactly one handler per extension. The handler is invisible; the window
              that opens is Edge.
text.browser.title: Pick the browser, once
text.browser.lead:
Fenestra opens a normal tab in the browser you choose. The choice is saved and applies
          to every double-click from now on.
text.browser.first: Fenestra reads the system default browser on every open (the http association), so changing it in Windows is picked up immediately. Nothing is stored unless you pin a browser in settings.
text.browser.settings: Double-click Fenestra with no file to open this screen again.
text.browser.systemText: With --browser default, the operating system decides. To change what that means:
text.browser.win: Windows: Settings → Apps → Default apps → choose your browser.
text.browser.mac: macOS: System Settings → Desktop & Dock → Default web browser.
text.mac.title: Compile it yourself
text.mac.lead: Binaries exist for Windows and Linux, and Homebrew covers the macOS CLI. But you can build every one of them from source — and on macOS it is the only way: there is no notarized binary, Apple charges US$ 99/year, and Gatekeeper blocks unsigned downloads.
text.mac.s1d: The official installer is signed by Google, so macOS shows no warning. It is the only thing you install.
text.mac.s2d: git clone, or download the ZIP if you do not have git.
text.mac.s3d: The script builds the CLI and Fenestra.app, then re-signs the app after editing the bundle.
text.mac.s4d: Drag Fenestra.app to /Applications, right-click an index.html, Open with → Fenestra → Always.
text.mac.note: No Xcode, no Apple account, no US$ 99. Tested on a real macOS runner in CI (arm64); on Intel the build is native.
text.mac.brewNote: Installs the prebuilt CLI for arm64 and Intel. The Finder app still needs the build above.
text.under.title: Small on purpose
text.under.lead:
One C# file for Windows, and two small Go ports for Linux and macOS. No dependencies, built
          by compilers you already have — small enough to audit in an afternoon.
text.under.p1s: HTTP/1.1 on a TcpListener, bound to 127.0.0.1 only. Only loopback Host headers are accepted.
text.under.p2s: Normalized and confined to the served root. .. , : and ::$DATA are rejected, and so are symlinks that escape it.
text.under.p3s: FNV-1a hash of the folder maps to a port that is stored and reused, so localStorage survives.
text.under.p4s: Extensionless requests return index.html; missing assets still return 404.
text.under.p5s: A second double-click pings the running server and just opens another tab.
text.under.p6s: Exits when the Edge it started closes, or after four idle hours.
text.sec.title: Local means local
text.sec.lead:
Loopback only, no telemetry, no accounts, no remote code. It serves the folder you opened
          and nothing else — but every file under that folder is reachable, including dotfiles.
text.sec.note:
Do not point Fenestra at a directory that contains secrets. The full threat model is in
          SECURITY.md in the repository.
text.name.title: A window, not a browser
text.faq.title: Questions people actually ask
text.faq.q1: Does it work with any static site?
text.faq.a1: Yes. Any folder with an index.html is served as-is. Each folder gets its own stable port, so two apps can be open at the same time without fighting.
text.faq.q2: Do I need Node.js or any runtime?
text.faq.a2: No. Fenestra is a single ~120 KB executable built against the .NET Framework that ships with Windows. Nothing to install, nothing to keep updated.
text.faq.q3: Why does Windows ask me to confirm the .html handler?
text.faq.a3: Because Windows allows exactly one program per extension and does not let an app claim it silently. That is protection against exactly the kind of software that hijacks file associations.
text.faq.a4: No. It opens them read-only, serves them, and writes nothing to the project. The only state it keeps is a port number per folder, under %LOCALAPPDATA%.
text.faq.a5: The system browser is the default. Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium are detected automatically — plus Safari on macOS — and --browser edge pins Edge. It opens a normal tab in the browser you already use, so there is no engine to patch and no extra 150 MB.
text.faq.a6: No. It is a server that opens a tab in your browser. There is no address bar of its own, no tabs, no rendering engine. That is the point.
text.faq.q7: Will it run on macOS or Linux?
text.faq.a7: Yes. Linux has static binaries (amd64 and arm64) with a --install flag. macOS has no prebuilt binary: the macos/ kit builds on your machine, with no Apple account and no US$ 99/year notarization.
text.browser.safariNote: Safari is available on macOS only.
text.privacy.title: Privacy, in plain language
text.privacy.lead: Fenestra is a local tool. This site does not use cookies, analytics, advertising or tracking.
text.privacy.s1d: There are no cookies, pixels, fingerprinting, analytics or advertising scripts. Nothing is shared with third parties. The only external service involved is GitHub Pages, which serves this site.
text.privacy.s2d: Your browser may store two preferences in localStorage: the language you choose in the menu, and the fact that you dismissed the privacy notice. The language detected from your browser is not saved. You can clear both at any time in your browser settings.
text.privacy.s3d: This site is hosted on GitHub Pages. GitHub may process connection data such as your IP address for security and operation, under GitHub's privacy statement.
text.privacy.s4d: Fenestra runs on your computer. It does not send telemetry, usage data or the names of your projects. If version checks are added, they will be described here before being enabled.
text.privacy.s5d: You can clear the stored preferences at any time, block storage in your browser, or reach us through GitHub Issues. If you are in the EU, you also have rights under the GDPR.
text.privacy.notice: No cookies. We only store the language you choose.
text.pres.title: Fenestra, in one page
text.pres.lead: The official site and the manual condensed into one presentation you can read top to bottom.
text.pres.hero.title: Double-click. It just runs.
text.pres.hero.text: Fenestra is a tiny local server that turns any dist/index.html into a working site in your browser. No terminal, no extension, no custom browser.
text.pres.hero.meta: ~120 KB · MIT license · no .NET SDK · one file, no installer
text.pres.problem.title: The problem is the origin, not the file
text.pres.problem.lead: Modern builds use ES modules. Under file:// the browser treats the page as an opaque origin: modules are blocked, absolute paths point at the drive root, and service workers do not exist.
text.pres.problem.file: file:// — modules blocked by CORS, broken absolute paths, blank page
text.pres.problem.http: http://127.0.0.1 — modules load like production, SPA routes survive refresh
text.pres.flow.title: Three steps, none of them yours
text.pres.flow.1d: Double-click it, drag the folder onto the executable, or pass a path on the command line.
text.pres.flow.2d: It reads the HTML. Needs an HTTP origin? It starts a server on a stable port. Does not? It opens the file directly.
text.pres.flow.3d: A normal tab, in your window, with your profile, your extensions and your address bar.
text.pres.features.title: Everything that is inside
text.pres.features.lead: The same behavior the manual explains, item by item.
text.pres.f1d: The same origin every run: localStorage, cookies and the service worker survive.
text.pres.f2d: Extensionless routes fall back to index.html, so refresh works.
text.pres.f3d: Files that do not need an origin open directly, without a server.
text.pres.f4d: An entry under /src/ serves the sibling dist/, build/ or out/.
text.pres.f5d: Parent paths, drive tricks and hidden files are rejected or 403.
text.pres.f6d: Edge, Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, Chromium and Safari.
text.pres.f7d: Embedded in the executable, seven languages, opened with --manual.
text.pres.f8d: Stops with the browser it started, or after 4 idle hours.
text.pres.f9d: The only thing stored is the language you choose.
text.pres.f10d: A static version.json is checked once a week; one tab per version, dismissible.
text.pres.limits.title: What it does not do
text.pres.l1: No backend or API proxy — Fenestra serves files only.
text.pres.l2: No source compilation — use the project's own dev server.
text.pres.l3: No TLS or authentication — localhost only.
text.pres.l4: No notarized macOS app — the build kit compiles one locally.
text.pres.l5: Unsigned binaries — SmartScreen and Gatekeeper may warn once.
text.pres.cta.title: Audit, use, compile
text.pres.cta.text: The source archive at the tag, build scripts for every system, and checksums for every asset.
text.pres.closing: If it is useful to even one person, it was worth it.

html.hero.title:
Double-click.
It just runs.
html.hero.lead: Fenestra is a tiny local server that turns any dist/index.html into a working site in your browser. No terminal, no extension, no custom browser.
html.problem.lead: Modern builds use ES modules. Under file:// the browser treats the page as an opaque origin: modules are blocked by CORS, /assets/... resolves to the root of the drive, and service workers do not exist. The file is fine. The origin is not.
html.plat.win.run: Download Fenestra.exe and run it, or make it the .html handler.
html.plat.win.build: Build with build.ps1 using the csc that ships with Windows.
html.plat.linux.run: chmod +x fenestra-linux-amd64 and run it, or use --install to register the handler.
html.plat.macos.build: Go only — no Xcode, no Apple account, no quarantine after a clone.
html.install.def1: Right-click any index.html and choose Open with → Choose another app.
html.install.def3: Check Always use this app and confirm.
html.install.linux: On Linux there is a native build: one static binary, no Wine, no runtime. Download fenestra-linux-amd64 from the release and run it with chmod +x.
html.install.macos: On macOS there is no prebuilt binary: Apple notarization costs US$ 99/year. The macos/ folder is a build kit — install Go, run one command.
html.mac.nogit: No git? Download the ZIP, extract, and run bash build.command — the shell reads the script, so Gatekeeper is not involved.
html.name.lead: Fenestra is Latin for window: the opening, not the room. That is the whole idea — Fenestra does not render your site, it opens a window onto it and lets your browser look through.
html.name.p2: The word survives in Italian finestra, French fenêtre and Portuguese fenestra (the anatomical one), so it reads as "window" to a Romance speaker and as a proper name to everyone else. It is also a quiet joke: a browser is the frame; this is the opening.

meta.title: Fenestra — double-click a local site, it opens in your browser
meta.desc: Fenestra is a tiny local server for Windows, Linux and macOS that turns any dist/index.html into a working site in your browser. Edge by default; Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium supported.
